SURF: Steering the Scalarization Weight to Uniformly Traverse the Pareto Front

Can we choose weights that cover the Pareto front evenly?

Liuyuan Jiang, Chentong Huang, Lisha Chen

Acceptance reported on the author’s homepage.

Read the paperCodeVideo storyboard
The takeawayExplanationExploreEvidenceTechnical detailsVideo storyboardCite this work
The takeaway

SURF selects scalarization weights using an arc-length map of the Pareto front, so a limited solution budget can represent trade-offs more evenly.

The problem and the idea

A preference is an input to optimization. The distance between the resulting solutions is a property of the problem’s geometry.

A small budget makes spacing matter

Imagine training only a handful of models to represent different compromises between two rewards. If most of them end up near the same compromise, they spend computation on similar answers. The issue is visible even before deciding which model is best: the collection offers fewer distinct options than its size suggests.

Weights act through a geometry

A scalarization weight describes how a solver values objectives. It does not directly specify a location on the Pareto front. The solver and the problem jointly create the map from weights to objective values. This map can accelerate and slow down. Sampling the input evenly then produces uneven spacing at the output.

Measure distance before choosing the next input

The central idea is to change coordinates. Instead of asking for the next equally spaced weight, ask for the next equally spaced amount of distance along the front. Normalize cumulative distance to the interval from zero to one. Invert that cumulative map to recover the weights needed for those distance targets.

The map can be learned

The front is usually unknown before optimization. SURF reconstructs the map from solutions already obtained and uses it to choose the next weights. Repeating this process refines the map. The theory describes conditional contraction toward a floor caused by representing a continuous curve with finitely many points.

Read quality and coverage together

A collection can be evenly spaced and still far from the desired front. That is why the experiments report coverage alongside approximation quality. The practical question is whether a method uses the available solve budget to find both useful and diverse compromises. Objective normalization also matters because distance changes with the units of the rewards.

What the paper reports

Coverage and quality

The paper evaluates structured bandits, MO-Gymnasium tasks, and multi-objective LLM alignment. It reports coverage metrics alongside Pareto-front approximation quality. See Section 4 and Tables 1–2.

Source: primary paper
LLM alignment

In the reported Reddit summarization experiment, SURF improves hypervolume and spacing metrics compared with uniform weights under the same per-slot PPO budget. See Table 2 for the metrics, variability, and reward definitions.

Source: primary paper

Uniform coverage is defined using the objective-space metric. Rescaling an objective changes arc length, so objective units and normalization are part of the coverage choice. The convergence result also depends on the paper’s regularity and reconstruction assumptions.

A closer look

C(w) = ∫₀ʷ ‖r′(t)‖ dt / ∫₀¹ ‖r′(t)‖ dt; choose wᵢ = C⁻¹(qᵢ).

Here r(w) is the objective-space path induced by the scalarization weight w, and qᵢ are evenly spaced cumulative-distance targets. The rule requires a well-defined monotone arc-length map.

Read the technical scope

Under the paper’s hidden-space regularity and reconstruction conditions, the CDF estimation error contracts linearly toward a finite-sampling floor of order N⁻². N is the number of sampled solutions. This is a conditional approximation result for the reconstruction process.

Video storyboard

Production draft · approximately 2 minutes with diagram pauses · narration and storyboard, ready to record.

0:00–0:20

If we want an even spread of trade-offs, should we choose optimization weights evenly? That sounds reasonable. But weights are inputs, and solutions are outputs. The map between them can distort spacing.

On screen: Show eight evenly spaced marks on a weight axis, then eight unevenly spaced solutions on a curve.

0:20–0:45

As a scalarization weight varies, its solutions trace a path through objective space. The speed along that path is generally uneven. A small change in weight can mean a tiny change in one region and a large change elsewhere.

On screen: Animate a point moving slowly and then quickly along a Pareto front as the weight changes.

0:45–1:10

SURF changes coordinates. We measure cumulative arc length, normalize it into a CDF, and invert the map at evenly spaced distance targets. The resulting weights are chosen to spread solutions along the front.

On screen: Build cumulative distance, normalize it, and connect equal quantiles to unequal weights.

1:10–1:35

For structured problems, the map can be derived analytically. For general problems, SURF alternates optimization and map reconstruction. Under the stated regularity conditions, reconstruction error contracts toward a finite-sampling floor.

On screen: Alternate boxes labeled solve, reconstruct map, and sample next weights.

1:35–2:00

The experiments cover bandits, multi-objective reinforcement learning, and LLM alignment. Read coverage together with solution quality. The takeaway is that preferences need to be translated through geometry when our goal is an evenly spaced set of trade-offs.

On screen: Show the paper’s Table 1 and Table 2 headings, then the project link.
